clinicalPearls: Autoimmunity (development of autoantibodies or autoreactive T-cell responses against self-antigens) is present in essentially all individuals and tends to increase with age; it does not by itself imply disease. Autoimmune disease (AD) arises only when a loss of tolerance produces clinically relevant, pathogenic responses (p.2821-2822).

Roughly 150 organ-specific and systemic ADs have been described; in 2009 the U.S. prevalence was estimated at 7.6-9.4% of the population (about 25-31 million people), likely an underestimate, with an apparent ongoing rise in incidence and prevalence (p.2822).

ADs predominantly affect women and, as a group, rank among the top 10 leading causes of death in women; an affected person carries a higher risk of developing a second autoimmune condition, of autoimmunity in relatives, and of certain cancers and premature cardiovascular disease (p.2822).

AD is a multistep process: genetic and environmental factors drive immune dysregulation and loss of tolerance, and autoantibodies can be detectable years before clinical symptoms appear (p.2822-2825).

HLA haplotype is considered the best single predictor of AD risk; specific HLA-DR types, complement-component deficiencies, and genes in the type I interferon and B-/T-cell pathways raise risk, and many susceptibility genes (e.g., STAT4, PTPN22) are shared across several ADs (p.2822-2823).

Autoantibodies serve as diagnostic tools and, in some diseases, as markers of activity or worse outcome; however, for several autoantibodies a specific pathogenic role has not been established, and the relevant autoantigens of many ADs remain unknown (p.2825).

Natural autoantibodies are mainly IgM, encoded by unmutated V(D)J genes with moderate self-affinity, and are not pathogenic; the harmful autoantibodies of AD are high-affinity, somatically mutated IgG generated by somatic hypermutation, class switching, and antigen-driven clonal selection (p.2824-2825).

Dysregulated type I interferon signaling is implicated across SLE, primary Sjogren syndrome, and idiopathic inflammatory myopathies; neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation externalizes modified autoantigens and is implicated in SLE, ANCA-associated vasculitis, myopathies, antiphospholipid syndrome, and RA (p.2823-2824).

Many ADs are female-predominant; two X chromosomes (women, and men with Klinefelter XXY) increase expression of X-linked immunity genes such as TLR-7/8 and IRAK-1, and breakdown of X-inactivation has been linked to autoimmunity (p.2823).

Infections can both trigger AD and provoke flares via molecular mimicry, epitope spreading, bystander/adjuvant effects, release of hidden self-antigens, and epigenetic changes; EBV is linked to SLE, MS, RA, celiac disease, and Sjogren, and SARS-CoV-2 has been associated with myocarditis, new APS, MIS-C, Kawasaki disease, and Guillain-Barre (p.2825-2826).

Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) cause immune-related adverse events in up to 85% of treated patients (dermatitis, arthritis, thyroiditis, colitis among the most common); most are mild and overall survival/time to progression is generally not influenced by their occurrence (p.2826).
Drug-induced lupus is a well-recognized iatrogenic AD characterized by antihistone antibodies; in many cases discontinuing the offending drug is sufficient to abate symptoms (p.2826).
harrison.pathophysiology: Autoimmune disease reflects a failure of self-tolerance in a genetically predisposed host exposed to environmental and stochastic 'hits'. Central tolerance (deletion of autoreactive T cells in the thymus and high-affinity autoreactive B cells in the marrow) and peripheral tolerance (anergy from lack of costimulation, regulatory lymphocyte suppression, inhibitory costimulation, removal of autoreactive cells) normally restrain autoreactivity; impairment of these mechanisms allows pathogenic autoimmune responses. Susceptibility is largely polygenic (HLA-DR types, complement deficiencies, type I IFN-pathway and B-/T-cell genes such as STAT4 and PTPN22), with rare monogenic forms, and epigenetic programming (histone modifications, altered DNA methylation, trained immunity) further shapes risk. On the innate side, dysregulated or proinflammatory cell death (apoptosis, pyroptosis, necroptosis, NETosis) plus impaired clearance of dead-cell debris and defective nucleases prolong exposure of modified nucleic-acid autoantigens; endosomal TLR-7/8/9 and cytosolic sensors then drive type I interferon production and inflammasome activation. Plasmacytoid dendritic cells (major IFN-alpha producers), conventional dendritic cells, neutrophils/low-density granulocytes with aberrant NET formation, monocytes/macrophages with defective phagocytosis, and NK cells are all implicated. On the adaptive side, autoreactive CD4/CD8 T cells, Treg deficiency, and imbalance between costimulatory and inhibitory pathways (PD-1, CTLA-4) and cytokines (IL-2, IL-6, IL-17, IL-33) promote disease; pathogenic high-affinity IgG autoantibodies form immune complexes that deposit in tissue, fix complement, opsonize, engage activating Fc receptors, and drive type I IFN production. Inflammatory cytokines (TNF, IL-1beta, IL-6, IL-17, type I IFNs) sustain and amplify tissue injury. Female sex (sex hormones, X-chromosome dosage) and immune aging (inflammaging with senescent, proinflammatory cells) further potentiate autoimmunity.
additionalDifferentials: Organ-specific AD (e.g., Hashimoto thyroiditis, Graves disease, type 1 diabetes, pernicious anemia/autoimmune gastritis, myasthenia gravis, multiple sclerosis, vitiligo, autoimmune hepatitis, primary biliary cholangitis) (p.2822)
Systemic AD (SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, primary antiphospholipid syndrome, Sjogren syndrome, systemic sclerosis, idiopathic inflammatory myopathies, mixed connective tissue disease) (p.2822)

Systemic vasculitides (giant cell arteritis, Takayasu arteritis, polyarteritis nodosa, ANCA-associated vasculitis, anti-GBM/Goodpasture disease, cryoglobulinemic vasculitis, IgA/Henoch-Schonlein vasculitis, Behcet disease) (p.2822)
Paraneoplastic autoimmune syndromes (Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, paraneoplastic pemphigus, dermatomyositis, anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis with ovarian cancer) (p.2826)
Drug-induced lupus (antihistone-antibody positive) and immune checkpoint inhibitor-related immune adverse events (p.2826)
infectionMimics: Infections that trigger or mimic autoimmune flares: group A streptococcal infection underlying rheumatic fever via M-protein/myosin cross-reactivity (p.2825)
Coxsackievirus (myocarditis, Hashimoto thyroiditis, T1DM) and influenza A (T1DM, IgA vasculitis) as proposed autoimmune triggers (p.2825)
Epstein-Barr virus linked to SLE, MS, RA, celiac disease, and Sjogren syndrome (p.2825)
SARS-CoV-2-associated myocarditis, antiphospholipid syndrome, MIS-C, Kawasaki disease, and Guillain-Barre syndrome (p.2826)
nonInfectiousMimics: Paraneoplastic syndromes presenting before a cancer diagnosis (e.g., dermatomyositis, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, immune thrombocytopenia, vitiligo, thyroiditis) (p.2826)
Drug-induced autoimmunity from antibiotics, antihypertensives, antiarrhythmics, TNF inhibitors, antiseizure agents (p.2826)
Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia and mast-cell activation disorders presenting with multisystem symptoms (contextual, adjacent chapter) (p.2821)
additionalInvestigations: Disease-specific autoantibody panels: anti-dsDNA and anti-RNP (SLE); anti-Ro/anti-La and rheumatoid factor (Sjogren); ACPA, anti-carbamylated antibodies, rheumatoid factor (RA); anti-MPO and anti-PR3 (ANCA-associated vasculitis); anti-type IV collagen (Goodpasture) (p.2825)
Anti-TSH-receptor antibodies (Graves); anti-thyroid peroxidase and anti-thyroglobulin (Hashimoto) (p.2825)

Islet-related antibodies in T1DM: anti-insulin, anti-GAD (glutamic acid decarboxylase), anti-protein-tyrosine-phosphatase/IA-2; antibodies to multiple targets confer higher risk of progression (p.2825)
Anti-parietal cell antibodies in pernicious anemia (present in 70-90% of patients) and antimitochondrial antibodies (anti-pyruvate dehydrogenase) in primary biliary cholangitis (p.2825)
Myositis-specific antibodies (anti-aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase, anti-Mi2, anti-MDA5, anti-TIF1-gamma, anti-HMGCR, anti-cN1A) for risk stratification in inflammatory myopathies (p.2825)
Antihistone antibodies for suspected drug-induced lupus (p.2826)
Serum tryptase, 24-h urinary 5-HIAA, and metanephrines to exclude mast-cell, carcinoid, and pheochromocytoma mimics when relevant (contextual) (p.2821)
redFlags: New autoimmune-pattern symptoms in a patient on an immune checkpoint inhibitor (irAE such as colitis, thyroiditis, arthritis, dermatitis) — can be severe and may persist after stopping therapy (p.2826)
Sudden new autoimmunity or autoantibody synthesis following SARS-CoV-2 or other viral infection (APS, myocarditis, MIS-C, Guillain-Barre) (p.2826)
Autoimmune presentation that may herald an occult malignancy (paraneoplastic syndromes often precede cancer diagnosis) (p.2826)
Anti-Ro-positive pregnancy: IgG anti-Ro crosses the placenta and can cause neonatal lupus and congenital heart block in the fetus (p.2825)
Multiple positive autoantibody specificities (e.g., several islet antibodies in at-risk individuals) signaling high likelihood of progression to overt disease (p.2825)
harrison.prognosis: ADs are described as chronic, incurable conditions that significantly impair quality of life and, in many cases, carry accelerated mortality; as a group they are among the top 10 leading causes of death in women. An individual with one AD has elevated risk of additional autoimmune conditions, certain cancers, and premature cardiovascular disease. Autoantibodies (e.g., ACPA in RA, islet antibodies in T1DM, antimitochondrial antibodies in PBC) may precede clinical disease by years to a decade and can mark worse prognosis. Better understanding of pathophysiology is hoped to enable primary or secondary prevention (e.g., trials of oral insulin in T1DM-autoantibody-positive infants and at-risk RA studies), though more data are needed (p.2822, p.2825-2826).
pitfalls: Equating autoimmunity with autoimmune disease: autoantibodies/autoreactivity occur in healthy individuals (and relatives) and increase with age without necessarily causing disease (p.2821-2822, p.2825).
Assuming any detected autoantibody is pathogenic — several are used only as diagnostic or activity/outcome markers without a proven causal role (p.2825).
Overlooking that classification criteria (e.g., for SLE) were designed for clinical-trial enrollment, not for individual diagnosis (contextual, p.2827).
Attributing AD to infection on circumstantial grounds — causality is often unproven and supported mainly by animal models (p.2825-2826).
Missing iatrogenic causes: failing to recognize drug-induced lupus (antihistone antibodies) or checkpoint-inhibitor irAEs, where stopping the agent may resolve symptoms (p.2826).
harrison.severityClassification: No single unifying severity grading exists for autoimmunity as a whole; severity and classification are disease-specific and covered in the individual disease chapters. Autoantibody breadth/titer (e.g., number of islet antibodies in T1DM risk) and specific specificities (e.g., anti-TIF1-gamma marking cancer-associated myositis, anti-HMGCR statin-induced myositis, anti-cN1A inclusion body myositis) help stratify risk and outcome (p.2825).
management: Immunomodulatory therapy tailored to the specific disease: corticosteroids for acute control, conventional immunosuppressants (methotrexate, azathioprine, mycophenolate) and targeted biologics such as anti-TNF agents, B-cell depletion with rituximab and cytokine blockers
Symptomatic and organ-supportive care for affected systems, with physiotherapy and rehabilitation
Address modifiable environmental triggers, including smoking cessation, and mitigate accelerated cardiovascular risk
Monitor disease activity, autoantibody markers and treatment toxicity, with vaccination and infection prophylaxis for immunosuppressed patients
Surveillance for a second autoimmune condition and for the associated increased malignancy risk
Multidisciplinary specialist care coordinated by rheumatology and clinical immunology with relevant organ specialists
Counselling on familial risk given the shared heritable susceptibility
